issues.subcategory: fabricated/unsupported generalizability claim contradicting methods
issues.description: The discussion contains a sentence claiming the findings generalize to mixed-gender settings, but the study used exclusively sex-segregated chains (all-male or all-female). No mixed-gender condition was tested, so this claim is directly contradicted by the design and is logically unsupportable. It reads as an inserted, false statement.
issues.quote: These findings generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions used here, suggesting cultural transmission operates similarly in mixed-gender collaborative settings.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent sample size for 'no theory' group
issues.description: The text states the 'Configurations' treatment had 70 participants (14 chains x 5). In Figure 3 the 'did not inherit any theory' group is reported as N = 70, but participants who did not inherit a theory should exclude first-generation participants in the Configurations + Theory treatment AND should include only those who actually received no theory. Meanwhile the theory-inheritance breakdown (15+17+6+18 = 56) refers to inheritors in the Configurations+Theory treatment. The N=70 'no theory' group apparently equals the entire Configurations treatment, but first-generation Configurations participants also inherited nothing — the categorization of who counts as 'no theory' is inconsistent and not clearly reconciled across figures.
issues.quote: Participants who did not inherit any theory (N = 70) sampled various positions along each spoke (A)

issues.subcategory: unit inconsistency in speed values
issues.description: Speed is defined as '1m/descent time' and reported in m/h, yet the generation effect mean is reported as 5.37 m/h with a CI of (1.58, 9.02), while absolute speeds are ~123-154 m/h. A generation slope expressed in the same m/h units alongside first-to-last generation change of ~22 m/h (123.6 to 145.7) over 4 generations implies ~5.5 m/h per generation, which is roughly consistent, but the descent time of a 1m track at 145 m/h would be ~25 seconds — the unit definitions (1m/time giving m/h) and the switch labels '92 cm apart' versus '1-meter track' are internally inconsistent and unclear, undermining interpretability of all speed values.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed (calculated as 1m/descent time) increased across generations

issues.subcategory: track length discrepancy
issues.description: The introduction/results describe a '1-meter long inclined track' and speed calculated as '1m/descent time', but the Methods state the timing switches were '92 cm apart' and the task was to cover 'about one meter'. The actual measured distance (0.92 m) differs from the 1 m used in speed calculations, which would bias all reported speed values.
issues.quote: Two push-button switches (made from computer mice) were located 92 cm apart on the rails

issues.subcategory: undisclosed model selection degrees of freedom
issues.description: The authors state the final model was 'selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data' but do not report which models were compared, the selection criterion, or whether this was preregistered. This introduces researcher degrees of freedom that can bias inference, especially for the key preregistered speed analysis.
issues.quote: The final model specification was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data.

issues.subcategory: deviation from preregistered analysis due to non-convergence
issues.description: Preregistered analysis 4 was changed: the 'Physical Principle' term was dropped and scores aggregated because the preregistered model 'did not convergence.' Because the dropped term (physical principle and its interaction) is precisely the dimension central to the key claim about skewed/canalized understanding, aggregating it away could mask or alter effects. The deviation is disclosed (good) but the consequences for inference are not fully justified, and alternative convergence remedies were not reported.
issues.quote: As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable “Physical Principle” in the reported model.

issues.subcategory: exploratory analyses framed as confirmatory support
issues.description: The central narrative claims about theory transmission affecting exploration and understanding (Figure 3) are explicitly described as 'Exploratory analyses,' yet they carry much of the paper's interpretive weight and are presented with strong causal language. The preregistered confirmatory analyses (hypotheses 2) found no substantial effect of theory transmission on optimization/understanding; the strong conclusions rest largely on post-hoc subgroup analyses.
issues.quote: Exploratory analyses, however, reveal striking differences between treatments in participants’ exploration behavior (Supplementary Figure 1).

issues.subcategory: severely underpowered subgroups
issues.description: Key claims rest on very small theory-inheritance subgroups: only 6 participants inherited a 'full theory,' 15 an inertia theory, 17 a centre-of-mass theory. Conclusions about distinct exploration/understanding patterns (e.g., 'full theory produced compact and asymmetrical wheels') are drawn from N=6, which cannot support reliable inference.
issues.quote: The few participants who inherited a full theory (N = 6) produced compact and asymmetrical wheels (D-H).

issues.subcategory: causal claim from observational subgroup comparison
issues.description: Theory categories (inertia/centre-of-mass/full/irrelevant) were not randomly assigned — they emerged from what previous participants happened to write. Comparing understanding/exploration across these self-selected categories and attributing differences to 'inheriting a theory' confounds theory content with chain-specific trajectories and prior configurations. The strong causal language ('Inheriting an inertia-related theory increased their understanding of inertia, but decreased their understanding of centre of mass') is not warranted by this non-randomized contrast.
issues.quote: Inheriting an inertia-related theory increased their understanding of inertia, but decreased their understanding of centre of mass; symmetrically, inheriting a centre-of-mass-related theory increased their understanding of centre of mass, but decreased their understanding about inertia.

issues.subcategory: understanding measure may capture exploration history, not causal understanding
issues.description: The authors themselves note that the understanding test scores may reflect what configurations participants happened to explore rather than genuine causal understanding (Supplementary Figure 2 analysis). This undermines the central construct: the prediction-test score conflates causal comprehension with sampled experience, weakening the headline claim that 'understanding' did not improve and that theories reshaped 'understanding.'
issues.quote: However, participants’ understanding may also result from different exploration patterns.

issues.subcategory: 10-item test reliability and scoring not reported
issues.description: Causal understanding is operationalized via a 10-item forced-choice test (5 inertia, 5 centre-of-mass), but no internal reliability, item difficulty, or scoring scheme (e.g., how 'No difference' responses were scored, how the 0-10 or per-dimension scores map to reported means like 4.60) is fully specified. Without this, the understanding measure cannot be evaluated or replicated, and the apparent above-chance baseline interpretation is unclear.
issues.quote: The test comprised 10 pairs of wheels: 5 in which wheels varied in their moment of inertia, 5 in which wheels varied in the position of their centre of mass.

issues.subcategory: WEIRD, young, single-institution sample
issues.description: The sample is French university students aged 18-38 (mean 20.5) recruited from Lille. While the authors acknowledge WEIRD limitations for cross-cultural exploration, the broad conclusions about human technological evolution and archaeology are drawn from a narrow convenience sample performing a single artificial task, which limits external validity for the strong evolutionary claims made.
issues.quote: we asked successive ‘cultural generations’ of participants (French university students) to optimize a physical system

issues.subcategory: overextension from low-dimensional task to complex technologies
issues.description: The authors repeatedly extrapolate from a deliberately low-dimensional (2-variable) task to highly multidimensional real technologies (bows, kayaks) and to archaeological cognition. They even concede the canalizing effect is 'performance-neutral' only because of the 2-dimensional problem, implying their key mechanism may behave differently in the many-dimensional case central to their motivating examples — yet conclusions are generalized regardless.
issues.quote: these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations. This confirms that the retention of improvements over generations produces highly optimized solutions

issues.subcategory: no blinding of experimenter who positions weights
issues.description: The experimenter manually positioned weights on the physical wheel for each trial and was not blind to condition ('Data collection... was not performed blind to the conditions'). Manual placement introduces potential for systematic measurement error or unconscious bias in wheel construction/timing across conditions, with no inter-trial verification reported.
issues.quote: Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.subcategory: interpretation of CIs overlapping zero as confirmation
issues.description: Several reported credible intervals include zero or are very wide (e.g., generation effect CI (1.58, 9.02) is positive, but the understanding CI (-0.54, 0.25) includes zero and is interpreted as confirming no improvement). Treating a CI overlapping zero as positive evidence for the null (no understanding gain) confuses absence of evidence with evidence of absence; the preregistered hypothesis 1 'confirmation' partly relies on accepting a null from a wide interval.
issues.quote: while participants’ understanding did not (Generation 95% CI: (-0.54, 0.25), mean = -0.04, Figure 2.B)

issues.subcategory: marginal interaction interpreted asymmetrically
issues.description: The Generation x Treatment interaction for understanding has a CI of (0.03, 0.81) barely excluding zero, and is used to claim last-generation participants 'had a slightly better understanding when they had inherited a theory,' while elsewhere similarly marginal/overlapping intervals are interpreted as null. This inconsistent treatment of marginal intervals reflects interpretive flexibility.
issues.quote: Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (0.03, 0.81), mean = 0.44, Figure 2.B

issues.subcategory: non-descending wheels excluded from speed analysis without modeling
issues.description: Failures (wheels that did not descend) are a meaningful outcome but are handled by restricting analyses to the 'last two trials' to 'limit the occurrence' of failures, and speed lines show only non-failure wheels. Selectively analyzing successful descents and using failure-reduction as a data restriction criterion can bias speed estimates upward and is not modeled (e.g., via a hurdle/two-part model). The number and distribution of failures across conditions/generations is not fully reported.
issues.quote: Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset.

issues.subcategory: maximum/optimization baseline and 'random guesser' chance level unspecified
issues.description: The claim of '71% optimization' depends on MaxSpeed (~154 m/h) and a starting baseline, but how the 71% is computed (relative to what minimum/first-generation value) is not shown. Similarly, the 'expected score for random guessers' line in figures is referenced but the chance value is not stated given the three-option response (Wheel1/Wheel2/No difference), making the above-chance interpretation unverifiable.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h, these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.subcategory: MaxSpeed values differ between payoff and results
issues.description: The payoff equation uses MaxSpeed = 160 and MinSpeed = 96, but the results state the maximum possible speed was 'about 154 m/h.' These differing maxima (160 vs 154) are not reconciled, creating ambiguity about the true performance ceiling used for the 71% optimization claim.
issues.quote: with MaxSpeed  = 160, MinSpeed = 96.

issues.subcategory: confound from transmitted configurations vs theory content
issues.description: In the Configurations+Theory treatment, participants inherit both the previous participant's configurations AND theory. Because configurations themselves convey strong directional information (and theories were written based on those very configurations), the exploration patterns attributed to 'inheriting a theory' are confounded with the inherited configurations, which differ systematically across theory types. The design cannot isolate theory effects from configuration effects.
issues.quote: Participants who inherited an inertia theory mainly produced compact and balanced wheels (i.e. with low moment of inertia, Figure 3B and F).

issues.subcategory: overstated null effect of theory transmission given exploratory differences
issues.description: The paper concludes theory transmission 'has no noticeable effect on the pace of cultural evolution,' yet also reports striking exploration differences and downstream understanding effects from theories. The claim that theory transmission is inconsequential for optimization rests on a null from underpowered confirmatory tests while the exploratory results suggest substantial behavioral consequences — an internal tension between the abstract's strong null claim and the reported subgroup effects.
issues.quote: we find that the transmission of causal models across generations has no noticeable effect on the pace of cultural evolution

issues.subcategory: no descriptive statistics on theory content/length or irrelevant category
issues.description: 18 of 56 inheritors received 'diverse, irrelevant theories,' a large category that is essentially dropped from interpretation. The content, handling, and outcomes of this group are not analyzed, and how 'irrelevant' was operationalized beyond the inertia/centre-of-mass coding is unclear, leaving a substantial portion of the theory-transmission data uninterpreted.
issues.quote: 18 inherited diverse, irrelevant theories

issues.subcategory: small number of independent chains as true replication unit
issues.description: The unit of independence is the chain (14 per treatment). With only 14 chains per condition and 5 nested individuals, between-treatment comparisons and generation trends have limited power at the appropriate (chain) level. The justification ('larger than those reported in previous publications') is a weak basis for adequacy and no formal power analysis was conducted.
issues.quote: No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes (i.e. number of independent chains) are larger than those reported in previous publications

issues.subcategory: wheel-dynamics unfamiliarity assumption may not hold uniformly
issues.description: The claim that the task is 'unfamiliar' relies on a single 1990 study of Western students' wheel-dynamics understanding, yet participants reportedly had appropriate intuitions about maximizing acceleration (upper-right quadrant), and physics/engineering background was included. The assumption that participants 'cannot rely on acquired knowledge' is partially contradicted by their non-random, intuition-guided exploration.
issues.quote: it is unfamiliar (cognitive studies show that western students have poor understanding of wheel dynamics 15), so participants cannot rely on acquired knowledge to solve the task

issues.subcategory: incomplete reporting of priors and model diagnostics
issues.description: Bayesian multilevel models were fit with map2stan, but priors, number of chains/iterations, convergence diagnostics (R-hat, effective sample size), and posterior predictive checks are not reported in the main text. Without these, the credible intervals cannot be evaluated or reproduced.
issues.quote: We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R 32.  Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package 33 and 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences.

issues.subcategory: overreach to archaeological cognition
issues.description: The conclusion cautions against interpreting archaeological materials as evidence of sophisticated cognition based on a single lab task with a 2-variable artifact and university students. This is a substantial causal/inferential leap from a controlled microsociety experiment to claims about ancient hominin cognition and technology.
issues.quote: our experiment indicates that one should be cautious when interpreting complex archaeological materials as evidence for sophisticated cognitive abilities

issues.subcategory: ambiguous generation count (5 generations vs 4 cultural generations)
issues.description: The text alternates between '5 generations'/'After 5 generations' and 'four cultural generations' for the same optimization, which may be technically reconcilable (5 individuals = 4 transmission steps) but is presented inconsistently without clarification, creating ambiguity in the headline 71%-after-N-generations claim.
issues.quote: these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.subcategory: kappa reported only as aggregate with three coders
issues.description: Three coders coded theories, but only single Cohen's kappa values (0.81 inertia; 0.85 centre of mass) are reported. Cohen's kappa is for two raters; with three coders the appropriate statistic (e.g., Fleiss' kappa) and how disagreements were resolved into final codes are not specified, leaving the coding reliability procedure unclear.
issues.quote: Cohen’s kappa coefficients reveal almost perfect agreement between raters (0.81 for inertia and 0.85 for centre of mass).

issues.subcategory: trial restriction choice not preregistered/justified by data goal
issues.description: Restricting speed analyses to the 'last two trials' is justified post hoc as limiting failures, but this restriction is a researcher choice that conveniently uses the best-performing trials (later trials) and could inflate optimization estimates. Whether this restriction was preregistered is not clearly stated.
issues.quote: Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset.
